title: Bosveld Citrus grower system: first consultation

segments.text: Morning, everyone. Thank you for having me, and thanks for the coffee, Johan. Um, before we start, there's one thing I need to check with all of you. I'd like to keep a transcript of this meeting so I can write up the requirements properly afterwards. And I use an AI assistant that runs on my own laptop to help me sort through the transcript. Nothing goes to an outside service. Are you all comfortable with that?
Ja, that's fine with me.
Yes, no problem.
Fine by me. As long as it doesn't, uh, end up on the internet somewhere.

It won't. It stays on this laptop, and if anyone wants me to stop at any point, just say so. Okay. How was the road this morning, by the way? I came in on the R71 from Polokwane and the stop-and-go at the pass was terrible.
Ag, those road works. They've been there since Easter. My wife says they're building a new road one spade at a time.
It's worse in the afternoon. The trucks.

I'll leave early, then. Okay, so I've read the email you sent, Johan, but I'd really like to hear it from you in your own words. Maybe start with the co-op itself, and then what made you pick up the phone.

Sure. So, Bosveld Citrus Co-operative. We're in Letsitele, about twenty-five kilometres outside Tzaneen. We pack citrus for our members, mostly oranges, Valencias and navels, then some lemons, and a fair amount of soft citrus, the mandarins. The co-op was started in nineteen seventy-eight by eleven farmers.
Mm.

And today we've got, uh, about a hundred and forty member growers. Some of them are big commercial farms with a few hundred hectares, and some are small growers from the Nkowankowa side with five or six hectares. Everybody's fruit comes through the one packhouse, here, behind this office.
And the packhouse runs all year?

No, no. The season is, roughly, from the end of March with the early mandarins until about the middle of September, when the last Valencias go through. Outside of that we do maintenance, we do the books, and we argue about prices.
Mostly we argue about prices.

Ja, mostly. So what made me pick up the phone. Honestly, it's the growers. They phone us all day. Where's my fruit, what was my packout, when do I get paid, why did my bins get downgraded? And we can't answer them quickly, because the information is in, I'd say, five different places. And some of it is on paper.
Five different places. Can you walk me through them?
Precious can do that better than me. She lives in the packhouse.
Ja, okay. So it starts at the weighbridge. A grower's truck comes in, or a contractor's truck, with bins on the back. Each bin is about four hundred kilos when it's full.
Okay.
The truck goes over the weighbridge, and our clerk writes a delivery ticket. It's a carbon book, three copies. White copy for the grower, pink for the office, yellow stays in the book.
Handwritten?

Handwritten. The weighbridge has a little computer with the scale program on it, it's called WeighMate, and it prints the weight on a slip. Then the clerk copies the weight onto the ticket, with the grower number, the farm, the orchard block, the cultivar and the number of bins.
So the weight comes from the machine, but everything else is written by hand.
Exactly. Then the bins go into the holding area. They get a, uh, a cardboard tag tied on with the ticket number, and they wait for the line.
How long do they wait?
It depends. In the peak, sometimes two days. The early mandarins have to go through degreening first, in the rooms at the back, so it can be a while. The oranges usually go the next day.
Okay. And then?

Then the bins go onto the line. We've got an optical grader, the Optisort, that photographs every fruit and sorts it into classes. Class one for export, class two for the local market, and then juice. The grader's computer makes a report for each batch. A batch is basically one delivery ticket.
Right.
And the report says how many cartons of each class and the percentages. That's what we call the packout.
And the report lives on the grader's computer.
It lives on the grader's computer. Tannie Marietjie in the office prints them out every afternoon and files them, and then she types the totals into a spreadsheet.
My spreadsheet. Well, it's the co-op's spreadsheet, but I built it.
Okay. So Sipho, the spreadsheet is yours. What does it do?

So the spreadsheet is, uh, the heart of the whole thing, unfortunately. Every delivery is a row. Marietjie types in the ticket from the pink copy, and then she adds the packout from the grader report. And then at the end of each month I use that to work out the advance payments to the growers.
Advance payments meaning?

So in citrus you don't get paid the full price when you deliver. The fruit gets exported, it goes on a ship, it gets sold in Rotterdam or wherever, and only months later do we know the final price. So we pay the growers an advance. So much per carton of class one, so much per carton of class two, a few rand per bin of juice.
Mm-hm.
And then after the season there's a final pool payment, when all the money is in.
Right. So the monthly calculation is the advance, and the pool payment is once a year.
Once a year, usually in February. And that one's a beast.
I can imagine. And the growers, how do they find out what they've been paid, and why?

They get a statement. I make it in the spreadsheet, and Marietjie prints it and posts it, or emails it to those who have email. Some of them still come and collect it at the office, they like to have a cup of tea with her.
How long after the month ends do they get it?
Um, honestly, three weeks. Sometimes more. Because everything has to be typed first, and checked, and then I have to reconcile with the bank.
And that's when the phone starts ringing.
So the growers are phoning because they don't know where they stand for three, four weeks.
Exactly. And look, I understand them. A small grower with six hectares, that's his whole income for the year.
Ja.
He delivered thirty bins two weeks ago, and he doesn't know whether they packed out at eighty percent or forty percent. Of course he's going to phone.
How many calls are we talking about?
In the season? I'd say, uh, Marietjie gets forty, fifty calls a day. And I get the ones about the grading, maybe ten a day. Those are the angry ones.
Why angry?

Because when a batch packs out badly, the grower thinks we made a mistake. He thinks his bins got mixed up with someone else's. And sometimes, to be honest, they did. Because the cardboard tag fell off, or the ticket number was written badly and someone read a seven as a one.
Okay, that's important. How often does that happen?

Not often. Maybe, I don't know, two or three times a week in the peak. But every time it happens it's a big fight, and it takes a day to sort out. I have to go through the grader reports and the tickets and phone the driver.

Let me make sure I've got the picture. A truck comes in, it goes over the weighbridge, the clerk writes a ticket by hand with the weight from WeighMate. The bins get a cardboard tag, they wait, they go through the Optisort grader. The grader report gets printed, Marietjie types the ticket and the packout into Sipho's spreadsheet, and Sipho works out the advance at the end of the month and makes a statement.
That's it. That's the whole sad story.
And the fifth place? Johan said five.

Oh, the QC lab. Sorry. Before a grower picks an orchard, our lab tests samples. The sugar and the acid and the juice percentage, to see if the fruit is mature enough for export. Maturity tests. That's on paper too, and the results go to the grower by WhatsApp. Our QC lady takes a photo of the sheet and sends it.
Okay. And spray records? You mentioned export.

Ja, that's a sixth place, now that you mention it. Every grower has to give us his spray records before we can pack his fruit for export, because the European buyers test for residues. Those are in a lever arch file in my office.
So there's paper and spreadsheets everywhere, and the growers can't see any of it themselves. That's really helpful. What's the most painful part for you, if you had to pick one?
The phone calls. No, wait. The statements. Because if the statements came out in a week, half the phone calls would go away.
For me it's the typing. Marietjie types for, what, three, four hours a day in the season. And she's retiring.
When?
End of June next year. Right in the middle of the season, which is a whole other problem.
That's a real risk. Is there someone to take over from her?
Not yet. We'll advertise. But nobody else knows that spreadsheet like her and Sipho. She knows every grower by name, she knows whose son is farming now and whose wife does the books.
Okay. So let's talk about what you'd like. If this goes well, a year from now, what's different?

The growers can see their own deliveries and their packout on their phones, the same day or the day after. They get their statements in a few days, not three weeks. And we stop answering fifty phone calls a day.
Is there a number you'd want to hit? Fewer calls, faster statements?
Half. If the calls go down by half, I'd be happy. And statements within, let's say, five working days after the month end.
Five working days is tight, but, ja. If I don't have to wait for the typing, it's possible.
Good. I'll write those down as the goals. Precious, from the packhouse side?

For me it's the tickets. I want the weighbridge to be quicker, and I want the bins to be traceable without a cardboard tag that falls off in the rain. If every bin had a barcode or something, and you scanned it, then we'd always know whose fruit is on the line.
Do the bins have anything on them today? A number?

The bins belong to the growers, mostly. Some have numbers painted on, some don't. The co-op has about, uh, three thousand of its own bins that we lend out to the small growers, and those have numbers burnt into the plastic.
So putting a permanent label on each bin isn't straightforward.
No. That's why I said barcode or something. Maybe the barcode is on the tag, not on the bin. A plastic tag that you clip on, and it comes back to the weighbridge. I don't know, you're the expert.

I'm not sure I'm the expert on bins, but I'll look into what other packhouses do. Let me note that as something to work out together. So, scanning a tag at intake, and again when the bin goes onto the line.
Yes. At the tipper, where they tip the bins into the water. That's where we'd scan.
Hi, sorry, sorry. Is this the system meeting? Johan said half past nine, I think. Or I heard half past nine.
It was nine, Ruan. Come in, sit. Ayesha, this is Ruan, he does our IT. He's not staff, he's a contractor, but he's here every Wednesday, and whenever something breaks.
Hi Ruan, nice to meet you. We've just been through how a delivery goes from the weighbridge to the statement, and Precious was talking about scanning bins at the tipper.
Ah, okay. Ja, the scanning. Precious has been on about the scanning for a year.
Because it's needed.
No, I agree, I agree.
Ruan, it's actually a good moment for you. What's the network like? At the weighbridge, and at the tipper.
Uh, so. The office and the packhouse are on fibre, it came in two years ago, and it's okay.
Ja.

But the weighbridge is at the gate, about three hundred metres from the office, and it's on a wireless link, a point-to-point. When it rains hard, or when there's load-shedding and the battery at the gate runs flat, it drops. The tipper is inside the packhouse, so that's fine, the Wi-Fi in there is decent.
How often does the weighbridge drop?

In the season, maybe once a week, for an hour or so. And when the whole area's fibre goes down, which happens, someone digs up a cable next to the R36 or whatever, then everything's off. Last year we had a full day once.
So the weighbridge has to keep working without the network.
It has to. We cannot stop trucks at the gate. If a truck waits, the fruit sits in the sun, and the next twenty trucks are behind it on the road.
Okay. So the intake has to work offline and catch up when the link is back. I'll write that as a firm requirement.
Ja. And to be honest, I can put a bigger battery on the gate, that's not expensive. But the fibre outages I can't fix.
Let's talk about WeighMate for a second. Is it something you can get data out of?
WeighMate is old. It runs on a Windows PC under the counter at the gate. It writes every weighing to a little database file, and it can export a CSV at the end of the day.
Mm.
And I think the scale indicator is connected to the PC by a serial cable. So if you wanted the weight live, you could probably read it straight from the indicator, without WeighMate at all.
That's useful. And the grader, the Optisort?

That's the problem one. The Optisort was bought in twenty nineteen, from the supplier overseas, through their agent in Cape Town. Its computer is locked down. The reports come out as PDFs. There might be a database underneath, but we don't have the password, and the agent says if we touch it, we void the support contract.
So getting the packout out of the grader automatically is uncertain.
Very uncertain. I can ask the agent whether they have an export, a CSV or an API or something. They might want money for it.
Would you mind asking them? That's probably the biggest unknown we've got.
I'll ask. I'll send them an email this week.
Thank you. And if the answer is no, the fallback is someone typing the totals from the report, which is what Marietjie does now.
Or reading the PDF automatically? Can't a computer read a PDF?
Sometimes, if the PDF has real text in it and the layout never changes. I'd need to see a few. Can someone send me some grader reports from last season?
I'll send you some. Good batches and bad ones.
Perfect. And on the accounting side, Sipho, what do you use?

We use LedgerOne for the books. The payments to the growers go out through the bank, in a batch file that I upload to the bank's business banking. The spreadsheet makes the batch file, actually. Well, it makes a list, and I copy it into the bank's template.
So the payment calculation is in your spreadsheet, and LedgerOne gets the totals.
The totals, ja. I journal them in at the end of the month.
Would you want the new system to calculate the advances, or do you want to keep that in your spreadsheet for now?

Hmm. Honestly? Keep it in my spreadsheet for now. The rules change every season. The board decides different advance rates for different cultivars and sizes, and I don't want to phone a developer every time the board changes its mind. If the system gives me the deliveries and the packout, clean, I'll do the sums.
I agree. Let's not build the payment engine in the first round.

Okay, so that's a decision. The payment calculation stays in Sipho's spreadsheet for phase one, and the new system gives him the deliveries and packout as an export he can open in the spreadsheet. And then the statement. Does the statement come from the new system or from the spreadsheet?

Um. That's a good question. If the advance is worked out in my spreadsheet, the statement has to show the advance. So either I upload the amounts back into the system every month, or the statement stays in the spreadsheet.
Let's leave that one open for now. I'll come back with a couple of options. It depends on how much work an upload would be for you each month.
Okay.
Can we talk about the growers' information for a bit? What do you hold about them?

Names, ID numbers for the growers who farm as individuals, company registration numbers for the farms that are companies, VAT numbers, bank account details, physical addresses, phone numbers, email. And their delivery history, their packouts, and what they've been paid.
Okay. So for the small growers who farm in their own name, that's all personal information under POPIA, and the bank details need care in any case. Who should be able to see what?
A grower must only see his own stuff. That's the number one thing. If grower A can see what grower B got paid, I'll have a war on my hands.
Right.
Seriously. These people are neighbours. Their kids go to the same school, they sit next to each other in church.
I understand. So each grower sees only their own deliveries, packouts and statements. And in the office?

Me and Johan see everything. Marietjie sees everything except, no, actually she sees everything too. Precious and the clerks need the deliveries and the grading, but not the bank details and not the money.
I don't want to see the money.

So the roles are something like this. The office and management see everything. The packhouse staff see deliveries and grading, but not bank details or payments. And growers see their own. Who changes a grower's bank details today?
Only me, and only with a letter from the bank. Because there's fraud.
Mm.
Last year someone phoned, pretending to be one of our growers, and asked us to change his bank account. Luckily Marietjie knew his voice.
That's exactly the kind of thing to design for. So changing bank details stays a manual, checked process in the office, and a grower can't change them from their phone.
Definitely not.
Good. And the weights? What if someone changes a weight or a bin count after the fact?
That must be recorded. Who changed it and why. Because that's where the fights are.
So an audit trail on every change to a delivery: who changed it, when, what it was before, and the reason.
Yes. And the grower should be able to see that it was changed, I think.
Hmm. Maybe not the reason. Sometimes the reason is, you know, the driver counted wrong because he was in a hurry to get to the bottle store.
Okay, maybe not the reason.
I'll note that the grower sees that a delivery was corrected, and whether they also see the reason is still to be decided. Ruan, where would all this live? Do you have a preference for hosting?
Not on a server in the office, please. I don't want another thing to look after, and the power here isn't reliable. Some cloud thing is fine.
The board said the data must stay in South Africa. One of our members is a lawyer, and he was very firm about that at the last meeting.
Okay, so hosting in a South African data centre. That's a constraint, and it's possible with most of the big providers now.
Ja, they've got Johannesburg and Cape Town regions.
Exactly. And for the weighbridge, the tablet or PC at the gate would keep its own copy of the day's deliveries and send them up when the link is back.
And if the tablet gets stolen?
Good point. Then it should need a PIN or a login, and it shouldn't hold more than it needs. The day's deliveries and the grower list, not bank details.
Okay, that works for me.
How long do you keep the records now? Tickets and statements.
The auditors say five years for anything financial. The tickets we keep, uh, I think also five years, in boxes in the storeroom. The mice eat some of them.
Five years, then, for deliveries and statements. And when a grower leaves the co-op?
We keep his records for the five years, for tax, and then, honestly, nobody has ever thrown anything away.

That's common. I'll suggest that the system keeps a leaver's records for five years and then flags them for deletion, and you decide. Let's talk about the growers themselves. How do they use their phones? What kind of phones?

Everything. The big farmers have iPhones and laptops and their own farm managers. The small growers, a lot of them have cheap Android phones, and data is expensive. Some of them, the older ones, their kids do the phone stuff for them.
So whatever the growers use has to work on a cheap Android phone, on a slow connection, without eating their data.
Ja. And I don't want them to have to download an app. Last time somebody made us an app, for the, uh, the study group, nobody installed it. Twelve people, out of a hundred and forty.
A web page they open from a link, then. One they can save to the home screen like an app.
That's fine.
And SMS. Not everybody uses WhatsApp properly, but everybody gets SMSes.
What would you send them?
When their batch is graded. Your delivery number four four seven one packed out at seventy-eight percent class one, something like that, with a link to see the rest.
That's a nice one. Johan, are you happy with SMS?
SMS is fine. WhatsApp costs money if you do it through the business, doesn't it, Ruan?
Ja, it's per message, through one of the providers. But SMS also costs. About, I think, twenty-five, thirty cents a message.
Then let's say SMS for the grading notifications to start with, and maybe WhatsApp later. Are you all okay with that?
Ja.
Fine.
Good, that's decided. And how does a grower log in? Most of them won't want another password.
No passwords. They'll forget it and phone us.
One option is a code sent by SMS to the phone number you already have on file for them. They type the code, and they're in.
That works, if the number on file is right. Some of them change their numbers.
Then updating a phone number would go through the office, like the bank details, so nobody can take over someone else's account by changing the number.
Ja. Same rule.
Now, language. The growers speak?
English, Afrikaans, Xitsonga, Sepedi. Most of the small growers are Xitsonga speakers.
My mother would want it in Xitsonga. But she reads English too.
Do you want the grower pages translated?
Hmm. I don't know. It'd be nice. But the statements are in English now, and nobody complains.
The statements have to be in English for the auditors anyway.
So the minimum is English. Whether we also do Xitsonga, and maybe Afrikaans, for the grower pages, I'll leave open, and I'll tell you what it would cost to add.
Ja, let's see the cost first.
And how should it look? Do you have any preferences? Colours, style?
Our colours are orange and dark green. The logo is an orange with a leaf on it, use that. And big, clear writing. Some of our members are seventy, seventy-five.
For the weighbridge, big buttons. The clerk sometimes has gloves on in winter, and it's dusty. And it's outside, under the roof but outside, so the screen must be readable in the sun.
Would that be a tablet at the weighbridge, or the PC?
A tablet, I think. A rugged one. The PC is under the counter, and the clerk has to go inside the little office to use it, while the driver waits.
Then it needs to be charged every day, and with the battery at the gate...
We'll keep it charged, Ruan.
Okay, okay.

I'll write it down as a strong preference for a rugged tablet at the weighbridge, and I'll check the hardware cost. And for the growers, plain and simple: their deliveries, their packout, their statements, and not much else.
Not much else. If it's complicated, they'll phone us to ask how it works, which defeats the whole point.
When the truck leaves, does the driver still need a paper ticket?
Yes. The driver must leave with something in his hand, otherwise the grower phones to ask if the fruit arrived. A small printed slip is fine. Like a till slip.
So a small printer next to the tablet, that prints a slip for each grower on the truck.
Ja. And the SMS too, if they want it. But the slip, always.
The old ones like paper.
And if the tablet itself breaks on a busy morning?
We keep the carbon books in the drawer. Just in case. Then someone types them in afterwards.
That's sensible. I'll make sure there's a quick way to enter the paper tickets afterwards, so nothing gets lost.
Ja, keep the books. Tablets always die at the worst moment.
Okay. Let's talk volumes. How many trucks come through the weighbridge in a day?

In the peak, sixty, seventy trucks. Mostly between six and ten in the morning, because they pick in the, no, actually that's not right. They pick in the morning and they deliver late morning. Between seven and eleven, say.
And each truck carries how many bins?
It depends on the truck. A small grower's bakkie with a trailer, six bins. A big truck, forty bins.
Does one truck always carry one grower's fruit?
No, and that's another headache. The small growers around Nkowankowa share transport. There's a contractor, Mister Shirindza, with two trucks, and he collects from six or seven growers in one trip.
Right.

So one truck comes over the weighbridge with seven growers' bins on it. We weigh the whole truck, and then we have to split the weight by grower, by the number of bins each one has on the truck. The clerk does it with a calculator.
So one truck can carry several growers' bins, and the weight gets shared out. Is it always by the number of bins?
By bins. We can't weigh each bin separately, there's no bin scale. So it's the full truck minus the empty truck, divided by the bins, and each grower gets his share.
And the growers accept that?
They accept it because it's always been like that. Mostly.
I'll make sure the intake can split one truck's weight across several growers by their number of bins, and that each grower's ticket shows his own share. Does the contractor need to see anything?
No. The contractor gets paid by the growers directly. That's not our business.
So how many bins in a day, at the peak?
About eighteen hundred bins a day at the peak.
And how long does a truck take at the weighbridge now?
Four, five minutes when it's going well. The writing is what takes the time. When there's a queue, it backs up onto the road, and then the traffic department phones Johan.
Twice last season.
What would be good enough for the clerk?
Under a minute. If they can scan and tap and go, under a minute for the clerk's part.
So capturing a delivery at the weighbridge should take the clerk less than a minute, and it must keep up with seventy trucks in about four hours.

Ja. Oh, and sorry, I said eighteen hundred bins. That's what we do on a normal day in June, July. The peak last season, in the big Valencia week, was twenty-four hundred bins in one day. Twenty-four hundred.
Twenty-four hundred at the peak, and about eighteen hundred on a normal day in the middle of the season. Thank you, that matters for the sizing.
And it's growing. We've got two new members planting, and the old navel orchards are being replaced with mandarins, which means smaller fruit and more cartons per bin.
Any idea how much growth?
The board's plan says ten percent more volume a year, for the next five years. Whether that happens, with the prices the way they are, I don't know.
I'll design for that anyway. It's not a big number for a system like this. And how many growers would use the portal?
Well, all hundred and forty.

Johan, it's a hundred and sixty-two. A hundred and forty delivered last season, but we have a hundred and sixty-two members. The others haven't delivered for a season or two, but they can come back any time, and they still get the newsletter.
Ja, okay, a hundred and sixty-two. He's the one with the list.
So up to a hundred and sixty-two growers. And some will have more than one person logging in? A farm manager and the owner, say.
The big farms, yes. The owner and his manager, and maybe his bookkeeper.
So a few hundred users at most. That's small. The bigger load is the morning rush at the weighbridge, and the notifications going out after grading.
And when everybody opens their statement on the same morning.
Ja, that too. Still small numbers, but the pages should be quick on a slow phone. I'd aim for a grower's page loading in, say, three seconds on a 3G connection.
That's fine. Most of them have 3G at least. Some of the farms up towards the mountain have nothing, but then they come down to town.
Except after the hail. Did you hear, Ayesha? Last Saturday a hailstorm went right over Letsitele. Ten minutes. Some of the farms on the Rubbervale road lost half the crop on the trees.
Oh no. That's terrible.
My cousin's farm, a whole block of navels, all marked. It's juice now.
It happens every few years. That's farming. Anyway.
Johan, apart from the growers, what do you need to see as the manager? Day to day.
Every morning I want to know what came in yesterday. How many bins, per cultivar, and what the packout was. Right now I walk over to Precious and ask her, and she looks in her notebook.
It's a very good notebook.
It's a very good notebook. But when I'm in Johannesburg at the citrus meeting, I can't walk over.
So a daily summary for management: bins received and the packout, per cultivar, for the day before. On the phone or by email?
Both. An email at six in the morning would be perfect. And a page I can look at.
Okay. Any other reports? For the board, or for the export agent?
The board wants a monthly report. Volumes, packout, advances paid. I make that by hand too, in the spreadsheet, and it takes me a day.
That one I'd probably leave in your spreadsheet for the first phase, since the advances are there. But the volumes and packout could come straight from the system. Does that sound right?
That sounds right.
Okay. Precious, at the tipper, what happens when a bin is scanned? What would you want to see?
The grower, the block, the cultivar. And if it's the last bin of that delivery, so the line knows to close the batch on the grader. Right now the line foreman shouts.
He shouts?
He shouts. Last bin, four four seven one.
Okay.
And the grader operator types it in. If he doesn't hear, two growers' fruit go into one batch.
Mm. So the scan at the tipper should tell the operator when a delivery's last bin has gone in.
Yes. That alone would save me half my fights.
That's a good one. Can I ask about the clerks? How many people would use the weighbridge and tipper screens?
Two clerks at the weighbridge, one in the morning shift, one in the afternoon, and in the peak both together. And at the tipper, three people over the shifts. Plus me, plus the foreman.
And how comfortable are they with computers?
The weighbridge clerks, okay. They use WhatsApp, they use the WeighMate screen. The tipper guys, less. They'll want one button.
One button. I like that. Before we get to money. Have you looked at buying a packhouse system off the shelf?

We did, three years ago. There's a big one that the large packhouses use, from Cape Town. They wanted, I think, two million rand, plus a yearly licence, and it does a hundred things we don't need. For a co-op our size, it doesn't make sense.
And it didn't have the small-grower stuff. The sharing of trucks, the SMS.
That's helpful to know. So buying the big system was ruled out, mainly on cost.
On cost. And because the people who sold it never came back to us after the demo.
Okay. Can we talk about budget? Do you have a figure in mind?
The board approved, uh, six hundred and fifty thousand rand for the system. That was at the August meeting.
I'm not sure that's right, Johan. I think it was less.
Was it? I remember six fifty.
Six fifty was what Ruan's friend quoted us last year, for the app thing. The board approved something lower. Let me grab the resolution, one sec, it's in the file on my desk.
There he is. Did you find it?
Ja. Okay, sorry about that. Here it is. Resolution of the twenty-first of August.
Okay.

The board approves an amount of up to five hundred and eighty thousand rand, excluding VAT, for the development of a grower information system, and running costs of up to four thousand five hundred rand per month. So it's five eighty, not six fifty.
Five eighty. Okay, I stand corrected.

Thank you, Sipho, it's helpful to have it exactly. Five hundred and eighty thousand excluding VAT for the build, and up to four and a half thousand a month to run it. Does the four and a half include the SMSes?
It doesn't say. Hmm. I'd assume so. Everything it takes to run it.
Then I'll assume it includes the SMSes and the hosting, and I'll show you the monthly breakdown so you can check it against the resolution. Is the build amount for this financial year?
Our year ends in February. So whatever we spend before the end of February comes from this year's budget. After that, it would have to go to the board again.
Okay, that's good to know. That probably means paying in stages, with most of it before the end of February.
Ja, that would suit us.
And the export to your spreadsheet, Sipho. How do you want it laid out?
Per grower, per cultivar, per class, for the month. That's how my sheet works. If it's one row per bin, I'll drown.
Per grower, per cultivar, per class, for the month. Totals, not bins.
Totals. And the delivery numbers next to them, so I can check against the tickets if a grower complains.
And timing. When do you need it working?
Before the season. The first mandarins come in at the end of March. So, February?
February is too late for me. If the clerks must learn a new weighbridge system, I want them to practise in February. But there's no fruit in February. Hmm.
That's a real problem. There's nothing to practise on before the season starts.
We can practise with empty bins. Or, no, we can make up deliveries. Fake trucks.
Training with made-up deliveries in February, that works. So what's the hard date?
The intake at the weighbridge must be working by the first of March. The grower pages can come a bit later. The growers can wait until, say, the end of April for their first statements.
So two dates. The weighbridge intake live by the first of March twenty twenty-seven, and the grower pages by the end of April.
Ja.

That's about fifteen weeks from now, with the December break in the middle. It's doable for the intake if we keep it tight. But I want to be honest with you: the grader connection is the part that could slip, because we don't control it.
Understood. If the grader part is late, Marietjie keeps typing for a bit. It's not the end of the world.
When we start, what do we bring over from the spreadsheet? The grower list, for sure.
The grower list, with the orchard blocks and the cultivars. That's in a separate sheet, about six hundred blocks. Some of it's out of date.
Who could check it?
Marietjie. She'd know which blocks were pulled out and replanted.
And last season's deliveries? Would the growers want to see those on their pages?
Hmm. It'd be nice for comparing, this year against last year. But it's not essential.
The old data is messy, I'll warn you now. Different years, different columns. Some years Marietjie's niece did the typing.
Then I'd suggest we bring over the grower list and the blocks for sure, and last season's deliveries only if it's cheap, once I've seen the spreadsheet. We can decide that after I've had a look.
I'll send you a copy. Without the bank details.
Without the bank details, please. Just the grower numbers, names, blocks and the deliveries. That's all I need to see.
Ja, of course.
You mentioned spray records earlier, Johan. Do you want those in the system?
Ja, if possible. Every grower must give us his spray programme for each orchard before we pack for export.
Sure.
The European market tests for residues, and if one container fails, it's a disaster. For the whole co-op, not just for that grower. And our auditors check that we have the records.
How do the growers give them to you now?
Paper, email, photos on WhatsApp. Whatever they like. And my PA files them in the lever arch file.
So the growers could upload their spray records on the portal, for each orchard block.
Yes. And then, this is the important part, if a grower hasn't given us his spray records, the weighbridge must warn the clerk that this fruit can't go for export.
A warning, or does it stop the delivery?
A warning. We still take the fruit, it can go to the local market or to juice. But it must not go into an export batch.
Then I need to see it at the tipper too. When I scan the bin, it must say no export.
That's clear. So missing spray records mark a delivery as not for export, at the weighbridge and at the tipper. Do the auditors accept digital records, or do they want paper?
I don't know. I think digital is fine, but I'd have to ask them. Their next audit is in May.
Okay, I'll leave that as an open question for you to check with them.
I'll ask them.
Let's talk about the training a bit more. Who needs it, and when?
The weighbridge clerks and the tipper guys, in February, like we said. Two sessions, because of the shifts. And I want to be in both.
And me, separately, for the export to my spreadsheet. I don't need to know the weighbridge, I need to know my numbers are right.
That makes sense. A session for the packhouse team, twice, and one for the office. And a few practice days with made-up trucks.
Ja. And on the first real day, the first of March or whenever the first mandarins come, I want you here. Or someone.
I'll be here for the first two mornings of the season. That I can promise.
Good. Because the first morning, something will go wrong.
Something always does. And the growers? How do they find out about the portal?
The AGM is on the eleventh of March. Most of the members come, for the lunch if nothing else. We can show it on the big screen there.
That's a good moment. And then each grower gets an SMS with a link, from the office, and Mister Baloyi helps the small growers who get stuck.
Ja. And Marietjie can help too, she'll still be here then.
She'll want a farewell with a cake in June, by the way. A big one. I'm just saying.
She'll get a cake, Sipho.
Precious, at the weighbridge, apart from the grower, the block and the bins, is there anything else the clerk writes down today?
The truck registration and the driver's name. For the gate security, so we know who was on the property. That's in a different book, at the guard hut.
Should that move to the tablet as well?
If it's on the same screen, yes. Then the guard doesn't need his book. But it's not the important part.
Okay, I'll include it as a small extra on the intake screen. And while we're talking about the season, does the packhouse work weekends?
Saturdays in the peak, until one o'clock. Never Sundays.
Then the grower pages need to be up on Saturdays too.
Ja, they must. Saturday morning is when the growers have time to look.
And the maturity tests, the lab?
Nice to have. The QC lady, Nthabiseng, she'd love it. But it's not the main thing.
Let's put that down for later, then, not the first phase.
Ja.

Oh, one more thing about the packout. Should the grower see the packout immediately, or only after I've checked the report? Sometimes the grader gets it wrong. The camera gets dirty, or the light changes, and I redo the batch.
Hmm. I'd say after you've checked.
But then I'm the bottleneck. In the peak I'm checking sixty batches a day.
Ja. Well. Let's think about it.
I'll leave that one open. Whether the packout goes to the grower straight from the grader, or only after Precious has checked it. I can show you how both would work.
Okay.
Precious, when a grower disagrees with a packout, what should happen? Today he phones you.
Today he phones me, or he arrives at my office with his son.
Could the grower raise a query on his page instead? He presses a button on that delivery, writes what's wrong, and it lands with you, with the delivery, the scans and the grader report attached.
Yes. That would be much better. Then I have everything in front of me when I phone him back.
But he must still be able to phone. Some of them won't type.
Of course. The phone stays. The query on the page is an extra.
And I want to see how many queries each grower sends. Some growers query every single batch.
Mm.
I won't say who.
Ja, she won't. Ayesha, while we're on the growers, there's something I forgot earlier. The comparison.
The comparison?
Every grower wants to know how he did against the others.
Ja.
Was my eighty percent good, or was everybody on ninety this week? Right now they phone Precious and ask her.
And I tell them. Roughly. I say, ag, the Valencias from the lower farms were all around seventy-five this week.
So the grower would see his packout next to an average. The average of all the growers, for that cultivar, for that week?
Ja, exactly. But never another grower's name. Never. Just the average.

And only if there are enough growers in it. If there are two growers with, uh, hmm, wait. Say there are only two growers with lemons in one week. Then the average tells you exactly what the other one got.
That's a really good point, Sipho. So the average only shows when, say, at least five growers delivered that cultivar in that week. Otherwise it's hidden.
Five. Okay, fine. Five is fair.
I'll write that down. A cultivar average for the week, shown only when at least five growers are in it, and never with a name.
Can I add something about the packout? The grader doesn't only give the classes. It gives the sizes too. The count, how many fruit fit in a carton.
And the growers care about the sizes?
Very much. The big sizes get a better price, especially the navels. And Sipho's advance is different per size.
Per size group. We have three groups, large, medium and small. The board sets a rate for each one.
So the packout the grower sees should show the classes and the size groups, and your export should have the size groups too.
Ja. Otherwise I have to go back to the PDFs anyway, and then what's the point.
That depends on what the grader can give us, of course. If the agent's export has the sizes, it's easy. If we have to read the PDFs, I need to check that the sizes are in them.
They're in them. On the second page. I'll send you some with the second page.
Thank you. Can I go back to the weighbridge for a minute? When a truck comes in full, you weigh it. Do you weigh it again when it leaves empty?
The big trucks, yes. In and out. The bakkies and the tractors with trailers, no. We use the weight we've got written down for that vehicle. The tare.
Where is that written down?
On a list stuck on the wall in the weighbridge office. The registration and the tare weight.
How often is the list updated?
Every month. No, sorry, it should be every month. Honestly, it's every season. At the start of the season we weigh every vehicle empty, and that's it.
So the system should keep each vehicle's empty weight, so the clerk doesn't need the list on the wall, and the big trucks still weigh in and out.
Ja. And it must remind us when a tare weight is old. Say, older than a month. Because a farmer puts new sides on his trailer, and suddenly it's heavier, and then he gets paid for wood, not oranges.
So a reminder when a vehicle's empty weight is more than a month old. Is that a hard stop, or a warning?
A warning. Then the clerk weighs that vehicle out, that time, and the new tare goes in.
Okay. And between the weighbridge and the tipper, there's the holding area. Do you need to know where the bins are in there?

Oh, yes. That's my other headache. The mandarins go into the degreening rooms. We have four rooms. They stay there two, three days with the ethylene. And the oranges wait in rows in the holding area, under the roof, with the forklifts going up and down. And sometimes a delivery gets forgotten in a corner, behind the others.
Forgotten?
Forgotten. Last season we found twelve bins of Nadorcotts that had been in the holding area for six days. They were soft.
Mm.
Juice. Straight to juice.
And the grower wanted to be paid for export.
And he was right, actually. It was our fault.
So it would help to see which deliveries are waiting, where, and for how long.
Yes. A list of what's waiting, oldest first, and in which room. And if something has been waiting more than three days, it must go red.
Who would tell the system that a delivery has moved into a degreening room? Is that another scan?
Hmm. The forklift driver. But he won't scan. He's got both hands on the forklift.
Could he have a tablet on the forklift?
Ruan, no.
Maybe the person at the door of the rooms. Let me think about that one and come back with options. I'm not sure yet where that scan should happen.
Okay. But the list, I want.
Just so you know, the Wi-Fi doesn't reach inside the degreening rooms. The walls are insulated panels. If someone has to scan at the doors, I'll need another access point there.
Good to know. How much would that be?
An outdoor one, with the cabling, maybe five, six thousand rand.
Ruan, the packhouse side. When there's load-shedding, what keeps running?

The packhouse has a generator. A big diesel one, it runs the line. It takes about, uh, thirty seconds to kick in. The Wi-Fi access points are on the generator too, but in those thirty seconds everything drops.
So the tipper scanner loses the network for half a minute.
Half a minute, and sometimes the access points take another two minutes to come back up. I could put a small UPS on them. That's maybe three thousand rand.
That would be worth it, I think. And the tipper screen should hold its scans for a few minutes if the network drops, the same as the weighbridge, and send them when it's back.
Ja, I'll price the UPS.
Just do it, Ruan. It's three thousand rand.
Okay, okay. I'll do it.
Who else needs information from you? Outside the co-op, I mean. You mentioned an export agent.

The marketer. Our fruit is sold by an export agent in Durban. Every week they want to know how many cartons we packed, per cultivar and class, and what's in the cold store waiting for a container. They plan the ships from that, so if our numbers are late, our fruit misses a ship.
Every Friday. No, sorry, Monday morning. They changed it this year. By nine o'clock on Monday morning.
And how do they get it now?
I make a spreadsheet and email it. It takes me an hour, an hour and a half, every Monday.
So a weekly report for the export agent, with the cartons packed per cultivar and class, ready by nine on Monday. Do they want a particular format?
They sent us a template. I'll send it to you.
Please. And the cold store, is that something you track today?
The cold store is pallets. That's a different thing. The pallets get a sticker with the pallet number, and the cold store manager has his own book.
Then I'd keep the cold store out of the first phase, and the weekly report has the packed cartons only, unless that's not enough for the agent.
Hmm. They'll want the cold store. But let's start with the cartons.
Okay. I'll note the cold store as something for later. Sipho, you said earlier that some of the numbers on file are wrong. How many growers do you think we have a good cellphone number for?
Hmm. Good question. I'd say a hundred and thirty, maybe a hundred and thirty-five. The rest, either there's no number, or it's a landline, or it's the number of someone who has passed away.
So about thirty need checking before the season.
Ja. And there's another thing. Some families share. Three growers, a mother and two sons, each with their own blocks and their own grower number, and one phone.
Mm.
The Mathebula family, for example. One phone for three grower numbers.
So one phone number can belong to more than one grower. When they log in, they'd choose which grower they're looking at.
Ja. But then the mother sees the sons' payments.
That's their business. They're a family. If they share a phone, they share.
Hmm. I'm not so sure. What if they fight?
Then they get their own phones.

Let me put that down as a question. When growers share a phone, does whoever has the phone see all of those growers, or does each grower need his own number? It touches the rule that a grower only sees his own.
Ja, leave it open. I want to ask the lawyer member about that one.
While we're on statements. What's on a statement besides the advance? Are there deductions?

The packing fee, per carton. The bin hire, for the growers who use the co-op's bins, that's thirty-five rand per bin per season. Transport, if they used our truck, but that's only a few. And the levies. And at the bottom, what he got last month and what he got this month, because they always compare.
Okay. Even if the statement stays in your spreadsheet for now, it'd help me to see one. To see what the growers are used to reading.
I'll send you a statement. With a fake name on it.
Perfect, a fake name.

You know what would be cool? Drones. My cousin is using a drone to count the fruit on the trees. Then you'd know before the picking how many bins are coming. He says it's quite accurate, within ten percent.
Not today.
He says this every meeting.
One day you'll thank me.
Actually, Ruan isn't completely off. Do you know in advance what's coming in tomorrow?
The big farms send me a WhatsApp the day before. Tomorrow, forty bins of Midknights from block seven. The small growers, no. They just arrive.
Would it help if the big farms could put that on their page, instead of on WhatsApp?
It would help me plan the line. But I don't want it compulsory. If they have to fill in a form, they'll just stop telling me.
Optional. Nice to have.

Then I'll keep it as a nice-to-have for a later phase, unless it turns out to be cheap to add. One more practical thing. For the first weeks of the season, would you be willing to run the old way and the new way side by side? The carbon book and the tablet, both.
Both? That's double the work at the gate.
It is. But it means that if something's wrong in the new system, you've got the paper to check against. And Sipho can compare the export with Marietjie's typing for the first month-end.
I'd like that, actually. For the first month-end, I want to compare. I'm not paying growers on numbers I haven't checked.
Hmm. For two weeks, okay. Not the whole of April.
Two weeks at the gate, and Sipho compares the first month. Agreed.
Good. Two weeks of both at the weighbridge, and a check of the first month's export against the spreadsheet.
But then I want an extra clerk for those two weeks.
We'll get someone. There's always a student from the college in Tzaneen looking for a few weeks' work.
The orchard blocks. When a grower replants a block, or pulls out navels and plants mandarins, how do you hear about it?
When he delivers mandarins from a block that was navels. Then Marietjie phones him.
Or the clerk writes the wrong cultivar, and it goes into the wrong batch.
Should growers be able to update their own blocks on their page? Say, block seven is now Nadorcott, planted in twenty twenty-five.
Update, yes, but someone in the office must approve it. Otherwise they'll make mistakes, and the spray records go with the block, so a wrong block means a wrong spray record.
So the grower proposes the change, and the office approves it.
Ja. Like the bank details, but less strict.
And the hectares?
Hectares, ja, we need those for the estimate. The board wants an estimate of the crop before the season, per cultivar. Every grower sends us an estimate in February, how many bins they expect.
How do they send it?
On a form. Paper. And Marietjie phones the ones who don't send it, which is most of them.
Would it help to collect the estimates on the growers' page?
It would help a lot. But I don't know if it's for this year. February is when everything else is happening.
Then it's a candidate for phase one if there's time, otherwise next season. I'll price it separately, so the board can see what it costs on its own.
Price it separately. Okay. What else do you need from us?

Can I raise a few things that worry me a bit, so you know what I'm thinking? First, Marietjie retiring in June, in the middle of the first season with a new system. A lot of the knowledge is in her head.
That's my biggest worry too.
Could she be part of testing it, before she goes?
Definitely. She'd want to. She's been here thirty-one years.
Second, the growers. If the small growers don't use it, the phone calls don't go down.
Ja. We'll have to do something at the study group days. Show them on their phones.
The extension officer can help. Mister Baloyi, he visits the small growers every second week.
Good, that helps a lot. Third, the grader, which we've talked about. And fourth, the internet at the gate, which the offline part covers.
And the gate battery, which I'll do.
And the gate battery. Thanks, Ruan.
Sure.
One more on POPIA. The growers will be getting SMSes, and their details will be on the new system. Do your membership forms say anything about how you use their information?
The forms are from two thousand and five. Nothing about POPIA.
I'm the information officer, apparently. I registered last year, the lawyer member made me.
Then it'd be worth updating the forms, or sending the members a short notice about the portal and the SMSes before the season. I'm not a lawyer, so I'd ask your lawyer member to look at the wording.
He'll enjoy that.
And how bad is it if the system is down for an hour in the season?
At the weighbridge, it can't be down. That's why we said offline. For the growers' pages, an hour is fine. A day is not fine, the phones start again.
So in the season, the grower pages should be up during working hours, say six in the morning to six at night, Monday to Saturday, and any maintenance happens at night or out of season.
And backups. Daily, please. And not only in the same place.
Daily backups, kept in a second location, also in South Africa.

Ja. And one more thing from me. The hosting account must be in the co-op's name. Not yours, not mine. The last developer had everything in his own name, and when he moved to Australia we lost the website.
Two years we had no website.
That's fair, and it's how I'd do it anyway. The accounts in the co-op's name, and I get access as long as I'm working for you.

While we're on my side of things. The tablets. I can get rugged ones from a supplier in Polokwane, I think about eight and a half thousand rand each. We'd need two, one at the weighbridge and one at the tipper, plus a spare. And the little slip printer, maybe two thousand.
Is the hardware part of the five eighty, or separate?
Hmm. The resolution says development. I'd say the hardware is separate, from the equipment budget. But I'd have to check with the auditor.
Put it separate. We buy equipment every year anyway.
Okay, I'll show the hardware as a separate line in the proposal, so it's clear either way, and Sipho checks where it goes.
I'll check. Don't worry.
Is there anything you know is coming that I should keep in mind, even if it's not for now?

Two things. There's talk of merging with the co-op in Hoedspruit, the Blyde co-op. They're smaller, about sixty growers. Nothing is signed, but it's on the board's table. If that happens, there'd be a second packhouse.
So the system should be able to handle more than one packhouse later.
Later. Maybe in two, three years. And the second thing is the export documents. Every container needs a pile of paperwork, and that's another spreadsheet.
Two spreadsheets.
Two spreadsheets. But that's for later.
And the pool payment, maybe, next year. If phase one works.
Okay, I'll note those for later, and I'll design the data so that a second packhouse doesn't mean starting over. What about the co-op's own bins? You said you lend out three thousand.
Ag, the bins. We lose about a hundred a year. Nobody knows where they are. Some of them are on farms, some of them are, I think, in people's gardens with tomatoes growing in them.
Not now, Precious.
Not now. But one day.
I'll note bin tracking as an idea for later, too. Okay. What do you expect from me, from here on?
A price. A fixed price, please. The board doesn't like open-ended things. Last time we paid by the hour, and the hours never stopped.
That's fine. A fixed price for phase one, with the grader connection priced separately, because it depends on what the agent says.
Good. And we want training for the clerks, and for Marietjie and Sipho, and a manual. A short one.
With pictures.
Training, and a short manual with pictures. And support during the first season?
Ja. Someone we can phone when it breaks on a Saturday morning in May. Because it will break on a Saturday morning in May.
That's a fair expectation. I'll include season support in the proposal, with its cost, so you can see it against the four and a half thousand a month.
Good. And before you build anything, I want to see what the growers will see. Pictures, or whatever you call them.
Yes. I'll design the main screens first, and we'll go through them together, with a few of the growers too, before anything gets built.
With a few growers, ja. Good idea. Mister Baloyi can choose some. And while you're building, I want to know where it stands. Every two weeks, a short update. Half an hour on Teams is fine.
Every two weeks, half an hour. I'll set it up, and I'll show you whatever is working by then, not slides.
Not slides. Good.
One more question from my side. Who at the co-op would look after the system day to day? Adding a new grower, a new clerk, resetting a tablet.
Hmm. Good question. Ruan? No, Ruan's only here on Wednesdays.
I can do the tablets. But not the growers.
Not me. I've got enough.
Let me think about that one. Maybe the new person who replaces Marietjie.
Okay, I'll leave it with you. It'd help to know before we start training, so that person is in the first sessions.
I'll come back to you.

Then I think that's a good place to stop. Let me run through what happens next. I'll send you a summary of today by Friday, and a proposal with a fixed price for phase one within two weeks. Ruan will ask the grader agent about an export. Precious will send me some grader reports. And Johan will check with the auditors about digital spray records, and think about who looks after the system.
That's right. Thanks, Ayesha. Good meeting.
Thank you.
Thanks, Ayesha.
Cheers, everyone.
